title: Quantum skyrmion molecule: two quantum skyrmions bound by coherent magnon exchange
abstract: Quantum skyrmions in frustrated spin-$1/2$ magnets are bound states of a few flipped spins in a ferromagnetic background. Using exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group calculations for the $J_1$--$J_2$ triangular-lattice model with easy-axis anisotropy $K$, we ask what happens when two such objects are brought together. The binding energy per flipped spin of a single skyrmion has a minimum at $\Nf^{*}=7$ for $K=0.02$--$0.04$, and skyrmions smaller than $\Nf^{*}$ do not exist as pairs: at any distance they coalesce into a single larger object, and pinning wells cannot prevent it. Two skyrmions of natural size, by contrast, form a bound molecule without pinning or external field, with binding energy $U\simeq-0.007J_1$ at $K=0.03$--$0.04$ and an equilibrium separation of $5.5$ lattice spacings that does not depend on $K$ or on the size of the simulation domain; at $K=0.02$, where the single skyrmion is itself marginally bound, the pair is unbound within our resolution. The two constituents keep their identity ($7+7$ flipped spins) and are coupled by a coherent exchange of magnons, visible as number fluctuations between the two halves of the domain in excess of those of two independent skyrmions and as in-plane spin correlations between the two skyrmion walls that reach $0.16$ across the gap. These correlations follow the vortex pattern of the two textures and lock their relative helicity, the quantum counterpart of the helicity-dependent interaction of classical skyrmions. We discuss the molecule as a self-assembled two-qubit element for skyrmion helicity qubits in a single layer.
summary: This work theoretically models the interaction between two quantum skyrmions in a frustrated magnet, finding that they form a weakly bound molecule. The binding is robustly characterized by excess number fluctuations and specific in-plane spin correlations, confirming a coherent magnon exchange mechanism. This suggests the molecule could function as a novel two-qubit element for quantum computation.
main_problem: The study investigates the binding energy and coherent coupling mechanism between two quantum skyrmions in a frustrated spin-1/2 magnet.
main_result: Two skyrmions of natural size form a weakly bound molecule with a binding energy of $U \simeq -0.007J_1$, mediated by a coherent exchange of magnons that locks their relative helicity.
method: The authors employed Density-Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) calculations and analyzed number fluctuations and in-plane spin correlations to characterize the binding.
model_or_system: The system is a spin-1/2 model on a triangular lattice with nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) interactions, subject to easy-axis anisotropy ($K$). Skyrmions are bound states of flipped spins ($N_f$).
key_observables: Binding energy ($U$), number fluctuations ($	ext{var}(n_A)$), and in-plane spin correlations ($\langle \mathbf{S}_{+i} \mathbf{S}_{-j} angle$).
important_parameters: Natural skyrmion size ($N_f^*=7$), binding energy $U \simeq -0.007J_1$, and anisotropy $K \in [0.02, 0.04]$.
main_assumptions: The analysis uses finite flakes embedded in a ferromagnetic background, and the free-pair binding energy is treated as an upper bound due to DMRG convergence limitations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the minimum binding energy for single skyrmions at $N_f^*=7$, compare probability distributions for bound vs. independent pairs, and show non-zero in-plane correlations across the gap.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the single skyrmion size using binding energy analysis, then calculates the interaction energy for free pairs, and finally uses fluctuation and correlation measurements to confirm the coherent magnon exchange responsible for the molecular binding.
why_interesting: The concept of a quantum skyrmion molecule and its use as a potential two-qubit element directly connects condensed matter magnetism with quantum information science, making it highly relevant for AMO/quantum optics researchers.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Flake geometries. (a) Discs of 31, 55, and 85 sites used for a single skyrmion. (b) Stadium of half-width r0 = 4.6 and length d = 16 (261 sites) used for the free pair. Gray dots mark the first shell of the frozen ferromagnetic background. The dashed lines delimit the central column C (x = 0); the regions A′ (x < 0) and B′ (x > 0) are used for the number dis- tribution P(nA) and the mutual information (Appendix B).

FIG. 2. Binding energy per flipped spin, e(Nf), of a single quantum skyrmion (DMRG, χ = 1000–1200) on the 55-site disc for K = 0.02, 0.03, and 0.04 (filled symbols), and on the 85-site disc for K = 0.03 (open symbols). The minimum at N ∗ f = 7 (dotted line) defines the natural size; its position is independent of K and of the flake, while its depth is not.

FIG. 3. Distribution P(nA) of the number of flipped spins in the left half of a stadium. (a) K = 0.20, Nf = 3+3 skyrmions placed at d = 2, 3, and 4 with weak wells (hw = 0.02): P(nA) is broad and has no peak at nA = 3; strong wells (hw = 0.4, dashed line) make it bimodal. The two skyrmions have coalesced. (b) K = 0.03, Nf = 7+7, free pair (hw = 0) on the 217- and 261-site stadiums: a sharp peak at nA = 7 identifies two skyrmions.

FIG. 4. Pinned pair at K = 0.03 (hw = 0.01, r0 = 3.7 stadiums). (a) Interaction energy U(d) = E(14) −2E(7) as a function of the well separation d; open squares, χ = 2000. Inset: U at d = 8 as a function of the pinning strength hw. (b) Weight P(nA = 7) of the 7+7 configuration, showing that the pair remains two objects at all d.

FIG. 5. Free pair (hw = 0, K = 0.03). (a) Local density of flipped spins, ⟨Sz i ⟩+ 1/2, in the Nf = 14 ground state of the 261-site stadium. (b) Column profile n(x) of the same state and of the single-skyrmion reference (Nf = 7) in the same stadium; the two lobes of the pair are 5.5 lattice spacings apart. (c) Three DMRG starts on the 217-site stadium end at different separations with monotonically increasing energy (in units of J1, relative to Efm); the lowest, at separation 5.5, is the ground state.
